content:
I have some code with definitions of all five Mathieu groups, as well as M_21, as permutation groups (each M_n is given as a Subgroup (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))). I also have a couple different definitions (by which I mean, group instances constructed from different objects, and MulIso's between them; M_21 is isomorphic to PSL(3,4) for instance); theorems for containments between them (e.g. M12 is isomorphic to the point stabilizer in the standard permutation action of M13, as a special case of being a subgroup); their group orders; and proofs of their simplicity. This included construction the (binary and ternary) Golay codes and showing that M24 = Aut(G24).

It was done autonomously by Aristotle and I've now been working on cleaning it up now. I was wondering if there are any other important facts I should ensure to be in there for completeness.

Also, I'm looking for ideas on how to break this into manageable PRs? Start with a file defining all the groups as permutations, and their group order computations, maybe? I can organize the code but if I make the PR with just the definitions I expect to be met with "but this isn't proving anything" :upside_down: , but at the same time just making a PR with one group at a time would make the whole code less well organized than it could be I believe.
Hi, @Edison Xie and I have a project to define these, following Dixon-Mortimer, in a way which should make something mathlib-friendly, it would be useful to coordinate here.
Oh nice! We should. What would be best? A brief call later this week maybe?
A technical question though - given that some of these proofs are sometimes computational, and this is Aristotle code, was native_decide used anywhere?

Initially yes, it actually came up as an obstacle too (it was using it "too aggressively" during development and running into >1hr build times because Aristotle doesn't put a time limit on native_decide's). I then told it to clean those parts up to be more pen-and-paper and it seems to have done a fine job of that!

I have been working on Mathieu 24 out of Conway's "3 Lectures on exceptional groups" (which develops the theory simultaneously with that of Golay 24 and is quite light on computation) but I am at a very early stage. I have not looked at Dixon-Mortimer, but the table of contents suggests it starts with Steiner systems, perhaps similar to the treatment in Aschbacher's "Sporadic groups". Is that correct?
I'm not familiar with Aschbacher, but other than that, yes, that's correct
